name: ThunderKittens (and the HipKittens AMD port)
production_evidence: Project states many AI companies use it for production-scale training and inference, naming Together AI, Jump Trading and Cursor - vendor-published with no third-party measurement
HipKittens became an official AITER backend in March 2026, i.e. it ships inside AMD's own inference kernel library
strengths: Models the hardware rather than abstracting it: tiles no smaller than 16x16 because a modern GPU 'is a manycore processor where each core can efficiently run ~16x16 matrix multiplies'
First-class access to the newest tensor-core paths - 'asynchronous WGMMA calls on H100 GPUs and TCGEN05 calls on B200 GPUs'

Solves what actually costs performance and is usually hand-written: shared-memory bank conflicts, TMA address generation, distributed shared memory, load-store-compute overlap, NVLink/NVSwitch transfers
Embedded in CUDA rather than beside it ('natively embedded into CUDA'), so it does not block access to anything it cannot express
Keeps pace with new silicon: 2.0 added Blackwell with MXFP8 and NVFP4, and a 2026-09-10 release added Vera Rubin with new PTX instructions
weaknesses: It is a header/template library, not a compiler or DSL, so this schema's compile-time and strategy fields describe it only loosely (template-instantiation, no autotuner)
CUDA-only for ThunderKittens proper; AMD users need the separate HipKittens project, which is a port with different primitives, not the same codebase
2.0 restructured the repository: kernels must now be compiled individually and the top-level Python package is gone - an upgrade is a build-system change, not a version bump
Ampere support is no longer actively supported ('While ThunderKittens should still work on Ampere, we do not plan to bring further support'), so the supported floor moved twice in a year
Every performance claim is self-reported by the project, with no third-party benchmark or methodology
notes: The strongest answer to the task's '2025-2026 kernel DSL that has become load-bearing', reading 'DSL' as the C++-embedded kind rather than the Python kind - ThunderKittens is what a frontier lab writes when Triton is not low-level enough. It sits deliberately between Triton and raw CUDA: high-level enough to express a full attention kernel in a page, low-level enough to call WGMMA and TCGEN05 directly. Compare w7k-tilelang (Python DSL, portable across three vendors) and w7k-modular-max-mojo (Python-shaped MLIR frontend) for the other two points on that spectrum. HIPPITTENS IS INCLUDED IN THIS RECORD RATHER THAN AS ITS OWN because its most valuable content is comparative: the authors state that core tile and bulk-compute interfaces carry over from TK to HK 'but decisions around memory access patterns, scheduling compute and memory, and ordering thread blocks within the chiplet architecture differ'. Chiplet-aware thread-block ordering has no NVIDIA analogue, which is the concrete content of why a ROCm port is not a recompile. It supports CDNA3 and CDNA4 and is now an AITER backend, so on AMD it reaches production through flops/amd-rocm-aiter-kernels rather than as a standalone library. autotuning is false: performance comes from hand-written primitives matching the hardware, not from a search. input_languages carries cutlass-cpp as the schema's term for a C++-template kernel library, which is the right shape but strictly these are not CUTLASS headers - a vocabulary stretch, flagged. The production_evidence line is explicitly vendor-published and unquantified, the same standard the existing flops/tilelang record applies to DeepSeek's 'close to hardware limits'. compile_time_seconds is null: these are headers, so compile time is instantiation cost inside the consumer's build, not a per-kernel number.
